title: OpenAI ships Daybreak Red Team and Defense Factory security agents
subtitle: At its Cyber at the Frontier event, OpenAI unveiled an AI pen-tester for web apps and a Codex-linked agent that drafts patches as draft GitHub pull requests.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI unveiled two cybersecurity products at its 'Cyber at the Frontier' event on November 12. Daybreak Red Team is an agent team that performs penetration testing on web applications. Daybreak Defense Factory consumes confirmed Red Team findings, traces each vulnerability through the codebase, drafts a fix, and opens a draft GitHub pull request for an engineer to approve. The products run on OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model. Red Team is accepting early-access requests; Defense Factory is a research preview that ships inside the Daybreak plugin for Codex.

The pairing closes a loop that security teams have wanted for years. Red teams and blue teams work the same application from opposite sides — one finds, the other fixes — and the handoff between them is usually slow and manual. Daybreak chains the two agents against the same codebase, with a human gate at the pull-request stage. Nothing is deployed without engineer approval. That gate is why OpenAI could ship the product at all, and it is the same pattern that the ChatGPT Wallet launch leans on one day later.

Daybreak follows OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber launch and the ExploitGym benchmark on November 7, Anthropic's CIDP open-source scanner in October, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon for cyber defenders. Every major lab is racing to field cyber agents against both offense and defense use cases, and governments are watching closely — the EU AI Office opened its first information requests into OpenAI and Anthropic in October, and voluntary frontier-review commitments are now a year old. The question regulators care about is not whether these tools help defenders. It is whether the same agent, pointed in the other direction, helps attackers more.

A takeaway for learners: Daybreak is a study in the human-gate design pattern. The agents do the slow, high-volume work — enumerating attack surface, chasing a flaw through code, drafting a candidate patch — and a person approves the one step that actually changes the system. That shape is going to become standard for any agent that touches production. If you are building one, start with the gate and design the agent around it, not the other way around.
